summary: Outlines an architecture for hosts attached to several networks at once. It introduces the Provisioning Domain, a consistent set of network configuration information, so a host can keep each network's settings separate and choose appropriately. It came from the Multiple Interfaces Architecture Design team.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone on both Wi-Fi and a mobile network collects settings from both, such as which DNS server to use. This document groups those settings into separate sets, one per network, so that a lookup never mixes a DNS server from one network with a web address learned on another.

questions: how does a device choose which network to use
subtitle: How devices manage multiple networks with separate configurations.

tldr.problem: A device attached to more than one network can mix up settings that belong to different networks, and it can end up using a network in a way nobody intended.
tldr.mechanism: The document introduces the Provisioning Domain, a consistent set of network configuration information, and gives a reference model that keeps each domain's settings separate and says how a node should pick one for a given connection.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational architecture, not a protocol: the mechanisms that would carry PvD information, such as new DHCPv6 options or Router Advertisement options, are left to companion design documents.

facts.label: PvD definition
facts.value: A consistent set of network configuration information

today: RFC 7556 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it stands as the architecture for the Multiple Interfaces work rather than a standard. The protocol mechanisms that would carry PvD information were left to companion design documents, and the document points at existing work on adding information to prefixes as something any new mechanism should coexist with.

sections.title: The Multiple Interfaces Problem
sections.content:
A node attached to several networks can run into two kinds of trouble: the configuration it holds for different networks conflicts, or it tries to use more than one network at the same time. Various techniques tackle these problems today, and the Multiple Interfaces Problem Statement in RFC 6418 describes the landscape, but issues still appear.

This document groups the problems enumerated in that statement into three categories. First, a lack of consistent and distinctive management of the configuration elements associated with different networks. Second, inappropriate mixed use of those elements during a particular network activity or connection. Third, use of a particular network that is not consistent with its intended use or with the intent of the communicating parties, which leads to connectivity failure or other undesired consequences.

The document gives an example of each. For the first, a single node-scoped list of DNS server addresses learned from different networks leads to failures or delays in resolving names from particular namespaces. For the second, an attempt to resolve the name of an HTTP proxy server learned from network A using a DNS server learned from network B. For the third, using an employer-provided VPN connection for peer-to-peer connectivity unrelated to employment.

The architecture answers the three categories in order. It introduces the formal notion of a Provisioning Domain, including identity for PvDs, and describes mechanisms for learning the intended associations between acquired configuration elements. It introduces a reference model for PvD-aware nodes that prevents the inadvertent mixed use of configuration information that may belong to different PvDs. And it provides recommendations on PvD selection based on PvD identity, together with connectivity tests for common scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sorts the trouble into three kinds: settings for different networks not kept apart, settings from different networks used together by mistake, and a network being used for something it was not meant for. Each has an example, and each gets its own part of the answer.

sections.title: What a Provisioning Domain Is
sections.content:
A Provisioning Domain is a consistent set of network configuration information. Classically all the configuration information available on a single interface comes from a single source, such as a network administrator, and can therefore be treated as one provisioning domain. In modern IPv6 networks multihoming can put more than one provisioning domain on a single link, and in some scenarios elements of the same PvD appear on multiple links. Typical information in a PvD learned from the network includes source address prefixes for connections within the domain, the IP addresses of the DNS servers, the name of the HTTP proxy server if there is one, the DNS suffixes associated with the network, and the default gateway address.

A PvD-aware node is a node that supports associating network configuration information into PvDs and using those PvDs to serve requests for network connections in ways consistent with the recommendations of the architecture. A PvD-aware application is an application whose code or configuration is explicitly aware of the notion of PvD.

The document distinguishes two kinds. Explicit PvDs are built from information a node receives from the network or from other sources that conveys the presence of PvDs and the association of particular network information with a particular PvD. Supporting them will likely need protocol changes or extensions, for example one or more DHCP options carrying the PvD identity and its elements, or a DHCP option carrying only the identity so that the associations are made by the respective protocols, for instance a Router Discovery option associating an address range with a PvD. Key exchange and tunnelling protocols such as the Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 in RFC 7296 are other possible delivery mechanisms, since they can carry host configuration information. Link-specific and vendor-proprietary discovery mechanisms may also be used, provided they allow the necessary elements to be discovered. In all cases, nodes must by default limit the lifetime of dynamically discovered PvD configuration to relevant events: if an interface media state change is indicated, previously discovered information for that interface may no longer be valid and has to be confirmed or re-discovered.

Implicit PvDs exist because deployment of new features in networking protocols is slow and many networks will not advertise explicit PvD information for the foreseeable future. When a PvD-aware node connects to such a network it shall automatically create separate PvDs for the configuration received, and it shall treat network information from different interfaces that is not identified as belonging explicitly to some PvD as belonging to separate PvDs, one per interface. In a mixed mode, where some of the networks on a link advertise PvD information and others do not, the node creates explicit PvDs from the labelled information and associates the unlabelled configuration with an implicit PvD for that interface.

PvDs and interfaces have no hierarchical relationship. Multiple PvDs may be simultaneously reachable over one interface, and a single PvD may be simultaneously reachable over multiple interfaces. For explicit PvDs the PvD ID is, or has a high probability of being, globally unique, and it must be possible to produce a human-readable form of it for the end user. For implicit PvDs the node assigns a locally generated ID with a high probability of being globally unique.
sections.plainLanguage: A Provisioning Domain is one consistent bundle of network settings: the addresses to use, the DNS servers, the proxy name, the suffixes and the gateway. A device that understands PvDs keeps one bundle per network instead of one long list for everything, so it never mixes a setting from one network with another.

sections.title: How PvD Information Reaches the Node
sections.content:
DHCPv6 and Router Advertisements are the two most common methods of configuring hosts, and both would have to be extended to convey explicit PvD information. The document sets out the topics that must be settled before such a mechanism is finalised.

One message or several. When information about several PvDs comes from the same configuration source, it can be sent as separate messages, one per provisioning domain, or combined into a single message. Combining is more efficient but can cause problems with authentication and authorisation, and with information that is not tagged with any PvD at all.

Securing the information. DHCPv6 and Router Advertisements both provide some form of authentication, so the source's identity and the integrity of the message content are covered. That is not the same as knowing whether the source is allowed to provide information for a given PvD. For that, there must be a mechanism for the PvD owner to attach an authorisation token or signature to the configuration information it delivers.

Backward compatibility. The extensions should be defined so that unmodified hosts keep working as they did before PvD information was added. That may mean duplicating some information so legacy hosts still receive it, and PvD-aware hosts have to be able to use legacy configuration sources that provide no PvD information. The document also asks that any new mechanism try to coexist with deployed mechanisms that add information to prefixes.

Updating and withdrawing. Information provisioned to a host may become outdated or superseded before the host would normally ask for updates, so the mechanism must be able to update or withdraw all or part of the information for a given PvD. For efficiency there should be a way to say that everything from the PvD has to be reconfigured, rather than updating each item one at a time.

IKEv2. IKEv2 is another widely used method of configuring host IP information. The provisioning domain could be learned implicitly from the Identification - Responder payloads that the IKEv2 initiator and responder inject during their exchange, with the IP configuration depending on the named responder identifier. Another possibility is a specific provisioning-domain identifying payload extension to IKEv2. All of the considerations listed above potentially apply to IKEv2 as well.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCPv6 and Router Advertisements are the usual ways a computer learns its network settings, so both would need new options to carry PvD information. The document lists what has to be decided first: one message or several, how to prove the sender is allowed to speak for that domain, how to stay compatible with older hosts, and how to withdraw settings that have changed.

sections.title: Three Example Configurations
sections.content:
The first example is a mobile node with two interfaces, one to the mobile network and one to a Wi-Fi network. When it is only connected to the mobile network it has one PvD, implicit or explicit. When it discovers and connects to a Wi-Fi network it has zero or more additional PvDs, typically one. Some existing operating system implementations allow only one active network connection, in which case only the PvDs associated with the active interface can be used at any given time. The mobile network can deliver PvD information explicitly through the Packet Data Protocol context activation process, so the node treats it as an explicit PvD, while a legacy Wi-Fi network that does not communicate PvD information is associated with an implicit PvD.

The second example is a node with a VPN connection. Establishing the VPN creates zero or more additional PvDs, which may be implicit or explicit. Routing to addresses reachable inside that PvD is set up through the VPN, while routing of packets to addresses outside its scope stays unaffected. If a node already has N connected PvDs, after the VPN session is established there will typically be N+1.

The third example is a home network and a network operator that runs several PvDs. An operator may use separate PvDs for individual services so that the services are designed and provisioned to be completely independent of one another. From the point of view of the home network and the node, the model is functionally similar to being multihomed to multiple upstream operators: each service the provider offers is its own PvD with its own information. The operator may provide a generic or default PvD, explicit or implicit, giving Internet access, and provision the additional services as explicit PvDs for subscribing customers. The number of PvDs an operator can provision is based on the number of independently provisioned services it offers, and the document lists real-time packet voice, streaming video, interactive video such as n-way video conferencing, interactive gaming, and best effort Internet access as examples.
sections.plainLanguage: Three worked examples show what the idea means in practice. A phone on mobile data and Wi-Fi gets one domain for each. A laptop with a VPN gets an extra domain for the VPN, and its routes to the office network go there. A provider can run one domain per service, so video on demand has its own domain separate from plain Internet access.

sections.title: The Reference Model for a PvD-Aware Node
sections.content:
It is assumed that the configuration in a single PvD is normally enough for a node to fulfil a network connection request, so there should be no need to merge information across PvDs. Even when a PvD lacks some needed configuration, merging information from a different PvD shall not be done automatically, because that typically leads to the problems in RFC 6418. A node may use other sources, such as local policy or user input, to construct a PvD in its entirety, to supplement learned PvDs with particular configuration elements, or to merge information from different PvDs when policy explicitly allows it.

Name resolution. The node may use one or several PvDs for a name lookup. It shall choose a single PvD when policy requires a particular one for a purpose, for example to download a Multimedia Messaging Service message using a specific Access Point Name over a cellular connection, or to direct enterprise application traffic to a VPN connection to the enterprise network; the choice can be made by matching the PvD DNS suffix against the fully qualified domain name being resolved, or by matching the PvD ID. The node may pick multiple PvDs when they are for general Internet connectivity and it is trying to maximise the probability of connectivity, in a manner similar to Happy Eyeballs in RFC 6555, performing lookups in parallel or in sequence. By default, a node uses information obtained via a name service lookup to establish connections only within the same PvD as the lookup results.

Next hop and source address. For each destination address obtained, the node performs a next-hop lookup among routers associated with that PvD, either by matching source address prefixes or specific routes against known PvDs, or by receiving an explicit PvD affiliation advertised through a new Router Discovery option. It then selects the best source address under the rules in RFC 6724, with the added constraint that the source address must belong to a range associated with the PvD being used.

Listening applications. An application that opens a listening socket is authorised by host policy to use a subset of the connected PvDs. For an application that is not PvD-aware, the operating system decides the authorised set and the preferred outgoing PvD. For a PvD-aware application, both the authorised set and the default outgoing PvD can be the common subset produced between the operating system policies and the set of PvD IDs or characteristics the application provides. For connection-oriented APIs the PvD of the initial incoming packet is remembered for the established connection and used for that connection's outgoing traffic. For connectionless APIs the host should provide an API so that a PvD-aware application can query the PvD associated with a packet. If the determined receiving PvD is not in the allowed subset for the application, the packet should be handled as if there were no listener.

Security policies. By themselves PvDs do not define security policies and cannot be used to communicate them. The host's own policies are applied after taking received PvD information into account. In a VPN scenario such policies could require the host to use only the VPN PvD for some or all of an application's traffic, the behaviour known as disabling split tunnelling or force tunnelling, or apply the restriction only to selected applications, the split tunnelling behaviour.

Connectivity tests. A PvD can look like a good candidate and yet give limited or no connectivity to the desired network, for example a PvD that only provides scoped connectivity unless the node authenticates through a web portal. The node may therefore run a connectivity test before using a PvD, and it shall do so and consider using the PvD only after validation. Ongoing tests are also required, since end-to-end connectivity can be disrupted during the session, for example by layer 2 problems or IP quality of service issues, so a monitoring function is needed to remove a PvD from the usable set if necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The reference model says a node should do everything for a connection inside one domain: look the name up there, pick the router and source address there, and only let an application listen there if policy allows. A domain that cannot actually reach the network should be tested before use and dropped again if it stops working.

sections.title: Trust and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Section 7 divides PvDs into trusted and untrusted. Implicit and explicit PvDs for which no trust relationship exists are untrusted, and only PvDs meeting the requirements of Section 7.2 are trusted. A trusted PvD needs two things: a trust relationship between the node using the configuration and the source that provided it, which is the authorisation part, and some way of validating that relationship, which is the authentication part. It shall be possible to validate the trust relationship for all advertised elements of a trusted PvD, whether they arrive as a whole in a single DHCP option or separately in supplementary Router Advertisement options.

Two validation mechanisms are described. In the first, the trust relationship is validated through cryptographic authentication combined with an identifier configured on the node. If authentication uses a public key mechanism such as PKI certificate chain validation or DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities, authentication alone is not enough, because in theory any PvD could be authenticated that way; the node also needs configuration that trusts the identifier being authenticated, and validating the authenticated name against a list of trusted PvD names on the node is the authorisation step. In the second, the trust relationship may be validated by the connection through which the PvD was obtained. A handset connected to a mobile network may know through the mobile network infrastructure that it is connected to a trusted PvD, and whatever mechanism validated that connection is the authentication part; being configured from the factory, or through operator or user preference settings, to trust the PvD is the authorisation part.

Because untrusted PvDs can carry misinformation, a node that implements PvD separation cannot assume that two explicit PvDs with the same identifier are really the same PvD. A node that makes that assumption is vulnerable to an attack in which, for example, an open Wi-Fi hotspot claims to be part of another PvD to draw traffic intended for it onto its own network. Since implicit PvD identifiers are synthesised by the node, the issue cannot arise with them. Assertions about reachability, such as those a PvD can make through mechanisms like RFC 6731, cannot be validated without a trust relationship and must be ignored when they come from an untrusted PvD, or traffic could be diverted from legitimate destinations to spoofed ones.

Section 8 names at least three forms of attack. Tampering with provided configuration information can easily be prevented by the message integrity features of the underlying protocol: SEcure Neighbor Discovery would detect tampering with Router Advertisement contents and the DHCPv6 AUTH option would detect tampering with DHCPv6 message contents. A rogue configuration source may advertise PvDs it is not authorised to advertise, for example a coffee shop WLAN claiming to be an enterprise, and this may also happen by accident when two sites pick the same identifier. To detect and prevent it, the client must be able to authenticate the identifier the network provides, which means having configuration that maps the PvD identifier to an identity and being able to authenticate that identity, and the network must supply information the client can use to do so, for example a PKI-based or DNSSEC-based trust anchor or a key remembered from a previous leap-of-faith authentication. Because PvD-specific information may reach the client from an upstream provider, the PvD container and its contents must in that case be relayed to the client unchanged, leaving the upstream provider's signature intact. Replay attacks, in which captured configuration is replayed on another link or at a later time, are avoided by including a replay protection mechanism such as a timestamp or a nonce inside the PvD container.
sections.plainLanguage: The security section warns about three tricks: altering the settings in transit, a rogue network pretending to be a domain it is not, and replaying old settings later. The first is handled by the integrity checks the underlying protocols already have. The other two need the node to be able to check who is speaking and to reject information it cannot verify.
